title: My home
goal: Show people where you live and say who owns what, using the one Romanian case that really changes the form of a noun: the genitive-dative.
bekal: name the rooms and furniture in your apartment and say where they are
show possession with genitive endings: *mașina vecinului*, *ușa camerei*, *camera lui Andrei*, *mașina Ioanei*
state the rent with hundreds and thousands

notes: **Mașina vecinului — thing first, owner after.** *Mașina vecinului* = "the car of the neighbor". What's new is only the ending on the owner: *vecinul* (the neighbor) becomes *vecin**ului*** (the neighbor's). No word for "of", no apostrophe-s — the ending does all the work.

**Camera lui Andrei.** A man's name can't take an ending, so Romanian puts *lui* in front of it. In the literal line *lui* is written "of": it means nothing except that the name after it is the owner.

**Doamnei, mașinii, orașului — three more genitives in this dialogue.** *Doamna → doamnei* and *mașina → mașinii* are feminine words; *orașul → orașului* is neuter, which behaves like a masculine word in the singular. The full pattern for all three is in the first grammar box.

**Patru sute de euro.** *O sută* (a hundred) has a plural: *două sute, trei sute, patru sute*. The *de* you know from unit 5 still appears after round hundreds. *Euro* itself never changes form, while *leu* still becomes *lei*: *patru sute de lei*.

**Pe masă without an article, la etajul doi with one.** The golden rule of unit 6 still holds: after a preposition, a bare noun loses its article (*pe masă, în bucătărie*), but as soon as it has a modifier — here the number *doi* — the article comes back: *la etajul doi*. Note that *etajul doi* is the second floor *above* the ground floor (see the box below). *Pe lună* = "a month", the same chunk as *pe zi* and *pe an*.

grammars.title: The genitive-dative — the ending goes on the article
body: Romanian has cases, but far fewer than the Slavic languages: for nouns there is only **one extra form** to learn, and it does two jobs at once — **genitive** (whose?) and **dative** (to whom?).
The ending attaches not to the noun itself but to the **definite article** you've known since unit 4. So the rule is: take the form with the article, then swap the article.
after: **A trick for feminine words: plural form + *-i*.** The feminine genitive singular is always built from the **plural**: *cameră → camere → camerei*, *masă → mese → mesei*, *fată → fete → fetei*, *mașină → mașini → mașinii*, *stradă → străzi → străzii*, *ușă → uși → ușii*, *cheie → chei → cheii*. That's why the vocabulary has listed plurals since unit 5 — now they pay off twice. Only words ending in a consonant + *-ie* start from the singular: *bucătărie → bucătăriei*, *chirie → chiriei*.

**A few common forms worth learning whole:** *tatăl → tatălui*, *mama → mamei*, *sora → surorii*, *doamna → doamnei*, *domnul → domnului*. The possessive just follows: *mașina tatălui meu*, *camera surorii mele* (*mele* is used because *surorii* is built from the plural — just learn the chunk).

**The second job: dative.** The same form answers "to whom?": *Îi dau vecinului cheile* = "I give the keys to the neighbor". The pronoun *îi* from unit 10 appears as a double. The dative gets full practice in unit 19; for now just know you don't have to learn the form twice.

grammars.title: Names, *unui / unei*, and little *al, a, ai, ale*
body: Not every owner has a definite article to attach to. Names and nouns with *un/o* have their own route — still short, still regular.

Example
Meaning

after: **After *unei*, the noun still uses its "plural" form:** *o vecină → unei vecine*, *o stradă → unei străzi*, *o colegă → unei colege*. After *unui* the noun doesn't change at all: *un vecin → unui vecin*.

**Al, a, ai, ale.** A genitive may only stand **right after** a noun with a definite article. When that condition isn't met — the thing has *un/o*, another word gets in between, or the thing isn't named — a little linking word appears that agrees with **the thing owned**: *un coleg **al** lui Andrei* (m), *o prietenă **a** Ioanei* (f), *doi colegi **ai** lui Budi* (m pl), *două prietene **ale** Ioanei* (f pl). Also: *Mașina este **a** vecinului* = "The car is the neighbor's".

The full rules for *al, a, ai, ale* are A2 material. For now learn the four examples above as chunks, and use the safe pattern that is always right: **thing with article + owner**, with nothing in between.

blocks.text: Almost all furniture is neuter (*pat, scaun, dulap, frigider*) and almost all rooms are feminine (*cameră, baie, bucătărie, sufragerie*). To say where things are, use the prepositions from unit 6 without an article: *Patul este lângă fereastră. Frigiderul este în bucătărie. Cheile sunt pe masă.* Once the owner is named, the article returns and the genitive follows: *pe masa lui Andrei*, *lângă ușa camerei mele*.

blocks.title: How Romanians count rooms
items: An ad for an *apartament cu două camere* does **not** mean two bedrooms. Every living space is counted, including the living room: two *camere* = one *sufragerie* + one *dormitor*. The kitchen and bathroom don't count.
A ***garsonieră*** is a one-room apartment — a studio. The cheapest option, and the one students hunt for most.
The ***parter*** is the ground floor; *etajul unu* is the floor above it. So Mrs. Popescu's *etajul doi* is the third floor by American counting (the second floor in British English).
Most people in Bucharest live in a ***bloc***, an apartment building. And shoes come off at the door: the host usually hands guests a pair of *papuci* (house slippers) right away.

sections.title: Renting an apartment — and the big numbers to pay for it

blocks.text: *Sută* and *mie* are ordinary feminine nouns, so the number before them takes the feminine form: **o** sută, **două** sute, **o** mie, **două** mii. Hundreds, tens, and units are simply lined up with no linking word — *și* appears only between tens and units, as in unit 5. As for *de*: look at **the last two digits**. If they are 01–19, no *de* (*o sută zece lei*); if 00 or 20–99, use *de* (*o sută **de** lei, trei sute cincizeci **de** euro, două mii **de** lei*).

blocks.title: Three things about renting in Bucharest
items: **Rent is quoted in euros and paid monthly.** This is the only place in the book where you'll meet euros; shopping, meals, and tickets are still in *lei*.
The ***garanție*** — a deposit, usually one or two months' rent — is paid up front and returned when you move out, if the apartment is in one piece.

On top of the rent come ***utilități*** (electricity, gas, internet) and ***întreținere***: the monthly building fee covering water, stairwell cleaning, and in winter the heating. Ask about both before signing the *contract de închiriere*.
